strengths: Original and well-motivated contribution: this is, to my knowledge, the first mechanistic interpretability study of how DiT-based text-to-image models implement multi-object spatial relation generation, unifying two previously separate strands of literature (cross-attention-based views and text-encoder-based views).

Well-designed controlled setting: the synthetic dataset (3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations, controlled occlusion, paraphrase variability) with a fully deterministic cv2-based evaluation pipeline enables rigorous, unambiguous measurement of four interpretable metrics (color, shape, binding, spatial relation), which is essential for the causal claims made.

Strong causal evidence for the RTE circuit: the paper does not stop at correlational attention analysis. Head ablation (L2H8: 67%→33% relational accuracy; L4H3: 90%→76% shape accuracy), VO-output injection from the relation head into positional embeddings (Fig. 5C), and QK-circuit analysis of sinusoidal positional embeddings jointly support a two-stage 'spatial relation head → object generation head' mechanism, and consistency is checked across model scales.

The T5 analysis is convincing within its scope: the token-masking ablations (relation words have little effect; shape2 masking harms binding/relation by 50%), variance partitioning with permutation significance testing (relation partial R² rising from 12.1% to 21.3% after DiT-MLP projection), and targeted vector arithmetic in the 4096-d embedding space that systematically reconfigures generated spatial relations provide a coherent, causally supported alternative account (information fusion in object-token embeddings).

The 'Attention Synopsis' method is a genuinely useful, scalable contribution for reducing the enormous DiT cross-attention tensor to an interpretable layer×head summary, and appears adaptable to other DiT interpretability studies.

The robustness finding (T5-DiT relational accuracy collapses ~40% with a single added filler word while RTE-DiT is robust, and vice versa for relation-word ablation) is an interesting, practically relevant dissociation between in-domain accuracy and out-of-domain robustness.
The appendix is unusually thorough: dataset generation pseudo-code, full encoder/training specifications, evaluation details, variance partitioning math, and prompt sweeps support reproducibility.
weaknesses: External validity is limited: all circuits are characterized on a toy task (10k samples, 128×128 images, 2 objects, tiny vocabularies) with models no larger than DiT-B. The discussion's claim that 'the embedding model could be the bottleneck for generating spatial relations in real-world scenarios' is plausible but speculative — no evidence is presented that the object-centric T5 strategy exists in real T2I systems (PixArt-alpha, SD3, etc.), and this limitation should be stated more explicitly.

Some unexplained anomalies weaken the experimental narrative: Table 2 shows T5 DiT-B WD collapsing to near-random accuracy across all metrics while T5 DiT-mini WD performs normally; also large systematic spatial biases (Dx, Dy around -35 to -47 px) for T5 models on perturbed templates. These are reported but not analyzed or explained, leaving questions about training stability of the T5 setup.

The robustness analysis is narrow: out-of-domain behavior is tested with essentially one perturbation type (inserting 'the'); a broader perturbation sweep (synonym swaps, reordering, additional modifiers, different paraphrase distributions) would substantially strengthen the generality of the robustness claims.

Several causal effects are modest relative to the narrative: e.g., ablating L4H3 reduces shape accuracy only from 90% to 76%, and the paper acknowledges effects confined to two heads, but redundancy/compensation by other heads is not deeply explored; also it is unclear how many independent training runs/seed replicates back the headline numbers (EMA averaging and 'averaged across multiple runs' is mentioned only for training dynamics).

Evaluation is heuristic: threshold-based cv2 parsing (intensity 180, area 100, 5-px tolerances, margin 25) is reasonable for this synthetic domain but brittle in principle; error rates of the evaluator itself are not characterized.

Presentation issues: 'casual manipulation' for 'causal manipulation' (Sec. 4.4), some dense figures (e.g., Fig. 5C, Fig. 8A) are hard to parse without the appendix, and the abstract's claim of 'near-perfect accuracy' sits uneasily with Table 2's sp rel+ values of ~0.62-0.75 for RTE models.

The claimed contributions are partially incremental relative to prior mechanistic work on diffusion models ([23,24]); the delta is the multi-object/cross-attention setting, which is real but the paper could engage more precisely with what is genuinely new methodologically versus contextually.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored question: applying mechanistic interpretability to spatial relation generation in text-to-image diffusion transformers. It usefully bridges two previously separate lines of work (attention-based remedies vs. text-encoder limitations) by showing that the choice of text encoder induces qualitatively different circuits.

The controlled experimental design is a strength: a synthetic dataset with precisely labeled shapes, colors, and relations, deterministic cv2-based evaluation of four orthogonal metrics (color, shape, binding, spatial relation), and models trained from scratch across multiple sizes and encoders. This allows claims about circuits to be checked rigorously.

The causal evidence is more thorough than typical interpretability papers: head ablations (L2H8 ablation drops relational accuracy 67%→33%; L4H3 ablation drops shape accuracy 90%→76%), VO-output injection of the relation head into positional embeddings to elicit selective attention (Fig. 5C), and targeted vector arithmetic on T5 embeddings that systematically reconfigures generated spatial relations while preserving object identity (Fig. 8B). The variance partitioning analysis (Tab. 1, App. B.6) with permutation testing is technically sound and well documented.

The Attention Synopsis method for reducing the enormous cross-attention tensor (layers × heads × steps × samples × tokens) to interpretable layer×head summaries is a practical contribution that could be reused for analyzing DiTs more generally.

The robustness finding (T5-DiT losing ~40% relational accuracy from adding 'the' to prompts, while RTE-DiT is robust to filler words but sensitive to relation-word ablation) is a genuinely interesting dissociation that links circuit structure to out-of-domain fragility.
weaknesses: Scope of external validity is narrow and the real-world claims are speculative. The dataset has 3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations, and a fixed caption template; the paper's own suggestion that 'the embedding model could be the bottleneck... making embedding model improvements potentially more critical than DiT modifications' is an extrapolation from this toy setting to frontier T2I models that is not tested (e.g., no analysis of PixArt-alpha, SDXL, or any pretrained model). This gap between the studied setting and the motivating problem (Fig. 10) is the paper's most material limitation.

Several central findings are close to predictable a priori: T5 contextual embeddings fuse sentence-level information, so relational information must live in non-relation tokens, and the DiT accordingly reads it from shape tokens; a bag-of-words encoder without positional encoding cannot distinguish argument order, so RTE-without-pos fails trivially. The interesting content is the confirmation and the specific head-level detail, but the headline conclusions are not surprising.

The identified circuit is demonstrably incomplete. Ablating L2H8 leaves 33% relational accuracy and ablating L4H3 leaves 76% shape accuracy, so a substantial portion of behavior is unexplained, yet the paper presents a 'minimal circuit' of two heads as if it largely accounts for generation. The residual mechanism is not characterized.

Key claims rest on essentially one model configuration. Circuit analyses (L2H8, L4H3) are presented for DiT-B; consistency across sizes is delegated to the appendix and the smallest model is simply excluded. The number of training seeds underlying the circuit analyses is unclear, and head specialization can be seed-dependent, which is not addressed.

Unexplained and potentially problematic results are left uninterpreted. In Tab. 2, T5 DiT-B WD collapses to near-zero on all metrics (e.g., shape 0.183 vs. 0.857 without WD), which is dramatic and unremarked. The text states the T5 relational accuracy drops 'by around 40%' under prompt perturbation, but the abstract claims it 'collapses'; the loose vs. strict metric discrepancy (e.g., 0.808 vs. 0.749 on the trained template but 0.498 vs. 0.306 on variants) also suggests sensitivity to evaluation choices that deserves more discussion.

The causal chain from relational tag to object generation is only demonstrated at the level of attention patterns (Fig. 5C shows elicited attention, not corrected generation accuracy), so the 'two-stage circuit' narrative is stronger than the evidence for the second stage.

Presentation needs substantial editing: 'casual manipulation' appears twice where 'causal' is meant; Figures 9A/9B are hard to parse (unlabeled model abbreviations, mixed trained/eval templates); Tab. 2 is dense and its template-variation structure is not adequately explained in the main text; several figures in the appendix have illegible axis labels.

Neither the synthetic dataset nor code is available at review time; the promise of release 'upon acceptance' limits reproducibility assessment for a paper whose value depends heavily on its analysis pipeline.

strengths: Original and well-motivated contribution: the paper applies mechanistic interpretability (circuit analysis, QK/VO decomposition, head ablation, causal manipulation) to multi-object spatial relation generation in DiT-based text-to-image models, a topic where prior work has largely offered correlational attention-map observations or encoding-side analyses; the framing that unites the 'cross-attention' and 'text encoder bottleneck' hypotheses via circuits is genuinely novel.

Careful controlled experimental design: training DiT models from scratch on a fully specified synthetic task (3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations, paraphrase variability), with ablations across three text-encoder configurations (T5, random embeddings with/without positional encoding) and four model scales, allowing clean localization of the relational computation.

Multi-pronged causal evidence for the RTE-DiT circuit: attention synopsis for head discovery (Sec. 4.1), QK-circuit analysis showing the relation head aligns positional embeddings with relation tokens (Fig. 4C), head-specific ablations (L2H8: 67%→33%; L4H3: 90%→76%, with other heads showing negligible effects; Fig. 6), and an injection experiment showing the object head reads the relational tag (Fig. 5C).

Interesting and well-supported finding for the T5 branch: token-level ablations (Fig. 8A), variance partitioning (Table 1) showing relation information is carried in shape-token contextual embeddings, and targeted vector arithmetic that causally reconfigures generated spatial relations (Fig. 8B) — a clean demonstration that T5 fuses relational information into object tokens.

Practically relevant observation that two mechanisms with similar in-domain accuracy differ sharply in robustness to small prompt perturbations (adding 'the' drops T5-DiT spatial accuracy ~40%, Table 2), with clear implications for the debate on text-encoder vs. DiT-side fixes.

Attention Synopsis is presented as a reusable tool for scaling attention-map analysis in diffusion models, and the appendix is unusually thorough (dataset pseudocode, evaluation pipeline, full training hyperparameters, variance-partitioning methodology with permutation tests), supporting reproducibility (code/data release promised).
weaknesses: Limited external validity: conclusions are drawn from a minimal synthetic world (two objects, three shapes, two colors, gray background) with models trained from scratch; the claim that 'embedding model improvements could be more critical than DiT modifications' for real-world T2I is plausible but extrapolated — no experiment on a pretrained large-scale model (e.g., PixArt-α or SD) tests whether the T5 object-token fusion mechanism holds beyond the toy setting.

The T5 circuit is comparatively under-characterized: the paper concludes 'no clear pattern emerges' from the synopsis for T5-DiT (Sec. 5) and relies on embedding-space analysis plus token masking rather than identifying an attention-level circuit; the asymmetry in rigor between Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 weakens the 'two contrasting mechanisms' narrative somewhat.

Ablation effect sizes are moderate and evaluated on a small prompt set (96/264 prompts): L4H3 ablation reduces shape accuracy only 90%→76%, leaving open how much of the behavior is distributed across other heads; residual capacity and redundancy of the circuit are not quantified.

Some findings are relatively predictable and add limited surprise: the failure of RTE without positional encoding follows directly from bag-of-words invariance of cross-attention conditioning, and the staged learning dynamics (attributes before relations) echo prior work [23, 24].

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies ('casual manipulation' for causal, 'andspatial', the abstract/intro describe eight relations while the dataset construction includes in-front/behind occlusion relations; Table 2 shows a catastrophic T5 DiT-B 'WD' configuration whose failure is not discussed); Fig. 9/Table 2 template-variation analysis would benefit from statistical uncertainty estimates.
The robustness analysis is narrow (essentially one perturbation type — inserting 'the'), so the sweeping conclusion about T5 brittleness and its real-world implications rests on limited evidence.

strengths: Well-designed controlled study: training DiT-based T2I models from scratch on a fully specified synthetic two-object spatial-relation task (with released pseudocode, rendering/annotation details, and deterministic cv2-based evaluation) enables rigorous, reproducible mechanistic analysis that is impossible on production models.

Substantive and novel findings: the discovery that circuit mechanisms differ drastically by text encoder (RTE: modular two-stage circuit with specialized spatial-relation head L2H8 reading relation tokens via QK/positional-embedding interaction, plus object generation head L4H3; T5/CLIP: object-centric decoding of relational factors fused into object token embeddings) is a clear, well-supported contribution that unites previously disconnected views of spatial-relation failure (cross-attention vs. text-encoder bottlenecks).

Claims are validated causally, not just correlatively: head-specific ablations (L2H8 ablation drops relation accuracy 67%->33%, L4H3 drops shape accuracy 90%->76%, with effects confined to the identified heads), VO-injection experiments showing downstream heads read relational tags, and direct vector arithmetic on factorized T5 embeddings that shifts generated object relations while preserving object identity.

Methodological contributions beyond this task: the 'Attention Synopsis' aggregation scheme for tractable analysis of the enormous cross-attention tensor, and the weight-space ramp-alignment head-screening method that identifies relation heads without generating images, both presented as reusable tools and demonstrated to transfer to CLIP-DiT and even a pretrained PixArt-Sigma model.

Interesting practical takeaway: in-distribution accuracy is similar for RTE- and T5-based models, but robustness to prompt perturbations differs markedly, and the T5 brittleness is mechanistically explained (perturbation shifts shape2 embedding toward relation factor directions, degrading the L3H7 gradient alignment from -0.98 to 0.45). The linkage of embedding design to interpretability, robustness, and inductive bias is a useful design insight.

The paper is generally clearly written with a logical structure (dataset -> benchmark comparison -> RTE circuit -> T5 circuit -> robustness -> discussion), and acknowledges limitations of the variance-partitioning factorization (zero-sum constraint bias) honestly.
weaknesses: Limited scope of the task and dataset: 3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations, 10k samples, fixed color-to-shape mapping (shape1 always red, shape2 always blue). The combinatorial space is tiny, so some findings may be artifacts of this regime, and the color descriptor is essentially redundant with shape1/shape2 ordering, which could simplify the binding/circuit analysis relative to what the narrative implies.

Ablation effects are partial rather than complete: ablating L2H8 only reduces relational accuracy from 67% to 33%, and L4H3 from 90% to 76%; the residual performance implies other redundant mechanisms or partially specialized heads exist, but the paper does not fully characterize what implements the remaining capability, so the 'highly concentrated circuit' claim is somewhat overstated.

The T5-DiT-B WD configuration catastrophically fails on all metrics (Table 2) and is never discussed or explained; this unexplained result leaves a gap in the model comparison, and the asymmetric behavior (mini with WD fine, B with WD broken) suggests the findings may be sensitive to hyperparameters in ways the paper does not address.

No error bars / significance reporting for most main-text experiments; multiple seeds are used for training-dynamics curves but the headline ablation and screening numbers appear single-run, which matters given that head specialization could vary across training runs.

Generalization of conclusions to real-world T2I models is indirect: the PixArt-Sigma experiment (A.10) is confined to one high-accuracy prompt and shows only weak spatial generation overall, so the central claim that 'embedding model could be the bottleneck in real-world scenarios' remains a plausible hypothesis rather than demonstrated fact.

Some presentation issues: several important analyses are relegated to hard-to-parse appendix figures (e.g., Figures 22-25 weight-screening heatmaps with dense numeric annotations); reference [9] is cited as arXiv 2025 in a manner inconsistent with the narrative timeline; Section C lists code/dataset availability but the actual URL appears missing/incomplete, weakening reproducibility claims at submission time.

The abstract/intro imply that RTE vs. T5 differences 'suggest the difficulty of generating correct relations in real-world scenarios,' but the toy prompts have no synonyms/ambiguity except hand-chosen paraphrases; the breadth of perturbations tested (filler 'the', sentence reversion, color synonym) is narrow relative to the generality of the conclusion.

strengths: Well-controlled experimental design: training DiT models from scratch on a synthetic two-object spatial-relation task allows rigorous, ground-truth evaluation of generation quality (shape, color, binding, relation) via a deterministic CV-based pipeline, which is a methodological advantage over probing black-box frontier models.

The paper goes beyond correlational attention analysis: findings are supported by head-level ablations (Fig. 4D, 5D), causal VO-injection manipulations (Fig. 5C), token masking (Fig. 7A), and embedding vector arithmetic that causally shifts generated spatial relations (Fig. 7C), giving the circuit claims reasonably strong causal support.

The Attention Synopsis and weight-space head screening (App. B.5, B.7) are sensible and potentially reusable tools for analyzing cross-attention in DiTs, addressing the practical difficulty of searching the huge attention tensor in diffusion models.

The comparison of random vs. T5 vs. CLIP text encoders is a genuinely interesting disentanglement: showing that similar in-domain accuracy is achieved by qualitatively different circuits (modular two-head circuit for RTE vs. object-token information fusion for T5/CLIP), and connecting this to differential robustness to prompt perturbations (Fig. 26-28), is a meaningful scientific observation.

Substantial supplementary material: dataset construction details, pseudocode, variance-partitioning formalism with permutation tests, and analyses across four model scales and three encoder families demonstrate thoroughness.
weaknesses: Limited external validity: the entire controlled analysis concerns 2 objects, 3 shapes, 2 colors, and 8 relations on 128x128 synthetic images. The central conclusion that 'the embedding model could be the bottleneck for generating spatial relations in real-world scenarios, making embedding model improvements potentially more critical than DiT modifications' is a strong claim extrapolated from a toy setting; the only real-model evidence (PixArt-Sigma, App. A.10) is shallow—one heavily cherry-picked prompt ('A dog is on the left of a human'), 8/30 object pairs with nontrivial accuracy, and no causal verification in the pretrained model.

Internal inconsistencies and unexplained results undermine confidence: the main text states DiT-B relational accuracy of 67% dropping to 33% after L2H8 ablation, but Table 2 reports sp rel of ~0.84 for RTE DiT-B; the T5 DiT-B with weight decay (Tab. 2) collapses to near-chance (~0.03) across all metrics with no explanation or follow-up; the abstract claims T5 accuracy 'collapses' under perturbation, which is more dramatic than the ~40% relative drop shown.

The robustness asymmetry claim could partly reflect training data statistics (RTE saw exact templates while T5's contextual embeddings may generalize differently) rather than circuit structure alone; the paper asserts a causal link between the single-token fusion circuit and brittleness (Fig. 27) but the evidence for this mechanistic account of perturbation sensitivity is suggestive rather than conclusive.

Reproducibility is incomplete: Section C ('Dataset and code availability') states all code and datasets are publicly available but the URL is missing/empty, so the reviewer cannot verify the release; given that the contribution is largely empirical analysis, this is a material gap.

Presentation quality is below par for CVPR: several main-text figures (Figs. 3-7) are dense and hard to parse; numerous typos ('casual' for 'causal', 'andspatial', 'it's'), and some claims (e.g., the embryonic-development analogy in Sec. 4.2) are speculative embellishments that add little.

The 'novelty' of the headline finding—that models with semantically meaningful embeddings distribute information across contextual tokens while models with random embeddings must compute the relation internally—is somewhat expected a priori; the value lies in the details of the circuits rather than a surprising discovery, which limits the paper's conceptual impact.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored question: how DiT-based T2I models implement spatial-relation generation internally, uniting two previously separate threads (attention-manipulation work [4, 26] and text-encoder-limitation work [18, 34]). The finding that the circuit differs drastically depending on text encoder (two-stage modular circuit with RTE vs. object-token-centric circuit with T5/CLIP) is a concrete, novel mechanistic insight.

The experimental design is rigorous for a mechanistic study: models trained from scratch across four sizes and multiple encoders, with a controlled synthetic dataset that admits exact, deterministic evaluation (cv2-based parsing with clear strict/loose criteria documented in App. B.4).

Causal support is strong and multi-pronged: head-specific ablations (L2H8 reduces relation accuracy 67%→33%; L4H3 reduces shape accuracy 90%→76%), VO-output injection showing L4H3 reads the relational tag produced by L2H8 (Fig. 5C), token masking in T5-DiT, and embedding-space vector arithmetic that causally shifts generated relations while preserving object attributes (Fig. 7C).

The proposed methodologies are generalizable contributions beyond this paper: the 'Attention Synopsis' for scalable cross-attention analysis over 10M+ attention maps, and the weight-space QK screening with ramp-template alignment that operates without generation, both validated across RTE/T5/CLIP models.

The robustness analysis is insightful and mechanistically explained rather than merely reported: adding 'the' biases T5-DiT toward lower-left generation, quantitatively traced via the ΔV shift aligning with relation factor vectors and cosine drop from -0.98 to 0.45 in the relation head (Fig. 27). This connects circuit structure to out-of-distribution failure, which has practical implications for embedding-model design.

Generality is supported by replication across model scales (DiT-B/mini/micro), across encoders (CLIP-DiT analysis in A.9), and partially on a pre-trained model (PixArt-Sigma, A.10). Detailed appendices including pseudocode, full hyperparameters, and the variance-partitioning formalism support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The controlled synthetic setting (two objects, 3 shapes, 2 colors, gray background, 128×128) limits external validity. The claim that 'embedding model could be the bottleneck in real-world scenarios' is plausible but remains an extrapolation; the PixArt-Sigma experiment (App. A.10) is suggestive but thin — in-depth analysis on essentially one prompt ('A dog is on the left of a human'), and no analysis of stronger pre-trained models like SDXL is attempted.

The evaluation pipeline relies on heuristic cv2 thresholding (intensity threshold 180, vertex counting, 100-pixel area cutoff, RGB margin 25). Errors in this parser could be conflated with generation failures; no manual validation of parser accuracy against ground truth is reported. Also, best models reach only ~80-86% strict relation accuracy, so a nontrivial fraction of scores mixes model error with measurement noise.

The variance partitioning / factor-vector extraction has acknowledged biases (sum-to-zero constraints forcing red/blue vectors to be exactly opposite, zero-sum relation vectors — admitted in App. B.6), and the vector-arithmetic manipulation uses an ad hoc scale factor (3V_rel); the sensitivity of conclusions to these choices is not ablated.

Some interpretation is somewhat speculative: the embryology analogy in Sec. 4.2 is decorative; the asymmetric 'object1' vs 'object2' head structure (single dominating L2H8 for object1, multiple heads for object2) is observed but not deeply explained.

Presentation issues: incomplete code-availability statement (Sec. C ends with a dangling URL), reference duplication [28]/[29], minor typos and grammar issues ('casual manipulation', 'andspatial', 'few work has'), and Figure 8 (benchmark context) is referenced before the appendix where it lives, weakening the motivation chain in Sec. 2.

The comparison of robustness between RTE and T5 circuits, while the headline practical finding, is based on a small set of perturbation types (insert 'the', reversion, synonyms); a broader perturbation distribution would strengthen the brittleness claim.
